summary: This FYI memo is a guide for newcomers to Internet Engineering Task Force meetings, explaining how the IETF works so first-time attendees can take part productively. It is informational and was replaced by RFC 1539.

eli5.summary: It is like a friendly handbook for your first day at a big club, explaining how things work so you do not feel lost. A newer handbook later replaced it.

questions: how does the ietf work for newcomers
what is the tao of the ietf
subtitle: A friendly 1993 field guide to how the IETF works and how to survive your first meeting.

tldr.problem: IETF meetings had grown so large that newcomers, about 38% of attendees at each meeting, struggled to get to know people and understand how things worked.
tldr.mechanism: The memo explains what the IETF is, how it is organized, how to register, which mailing lists to join, what to wear and how to prepare, with reference lists at the end.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational FYI document from January 1993 and was replaced by RFC 1539, so it is a snapshot of how the IETF looked then.

today: RFC 1391 is an Informational memo that was obsoleted by RFC 1539, so it should be read as a description of the IETF in January 1993 and not as current guidance.

sections.title: Why This Guide Exists
sections.content:
RFC 1391 is an FYI (For Your Information) memo, so it informs and does not specify an Internet standard. Its abstract says attendance at IETF Plenary meetings had grown phenomenally over two years. Approximately 38% of attendees were new at each meeting, and about 33% of those went on to become regular attendees.

When meetings were smaller, a newcomer could easily get to know people. The memo aims to explain how the IETF works so newcomers can make the meeting more productive for everyone, and it also supplies the mundane details every attendee should know.
sections.eli5: When lots of new kids join a club, they feel lost. This guide explains the rules and the people so everyone can join in.

sections.title: What the IETF Is and How It Is Organized
sections.content:
The memo describes the IETF as the protocol engineering, development and standardization arm of the Internet Architecture Board (IAB). It says the IETF is not a traditional standards organization and its Plenary meeting is not a conference. The IETF is the volunteers who meet three times a year. There is no membership: anyone may register and attend, and the closest thing to membership is being on the IETF mailing lists.

The Internet Society (ISOC), formed in January 1992, is the official parent organization. The IETF is divided into nine functional Areas: Applications, Internet Services, Network Management, Operational Requirements, OSI Integration, Routing, Security, Transport and Services, and User Services. The Area Directors and the IETF Chair form the Internet Engineering Steering Group (IESG), which gives the first technical review of Internet standards and handles day-to-day management. The IAB gives the final technical review.

Each Area has several Working Groups, which work under a charter toward a goal and usually disband once it is met. Birds of a Feather (BOF) groups are similar but have no charter and usually meet once or twice, often to see whether there is enough interest to form a Working Group.
sections.eli5: The IETF is a big team of volunteers split into nine groups by topic. Small teams inside each group work on one job and stop when it is done.

sections.title: Humble Beginnings
sections.content:
The first IETF meeting was held in January 1986 at Linkabit in San Diego with 15 attendees. The 4th IETF, in October 1986, was the first attended by non-government vendors. Working Groups were introduced at the 5th meeting in February 1987, and the 7th meeting in July 1987 was the first with over 100 attendees.

At the 14th meeting in July 1989 the IAB, then called the Internet Activities Board, changed its structure to leave only two Task Forces: the IETF and the Internet Research Task Force (IRTF). The IRTF considers long-term research problems.
sections.eli5: The club started with just 15 people in one room and grew year by year until it was very big.

sections.title: Registration, Mailing Lists and Meeting Etiquette
sections.content:
Everyone planning to attend should join the IETF announcements mailing list, where meeting information, Internet-Draft and RFC announcements, IESG recommendations and Last Calls are posted. A separate unmoderated discussion list exists for technical talk. Requests to join or leave a list go only to the matching -request address, never to the list itself.

Registration is by mail, email or fax. The early registration deadline is about one month before the meeting and carries a lower fee. Everyone pays the same fees, one person is allowed per form, substitutions are not allowed, and refunds carry a $20 service charge. The fee covers the Proceedings, the Sunday evening reception (cash bar), a daily continental breakfast and two daily coffee breaks.

On dress, the memo says the general rule is to dress for the weather, and that many newcomers are embarrassed to arrive in suits among T-shirts and jeans. Coloured dots on name tags mark people who volunteer for extra work, and newcomers are urged to talk to them. Attendees should also come prepared: read the documents the chair distributed and follow the Working Group mailing list. A Working Group is not the place to go for training.

The memo says that meetings are not a trade show: vendors should not try to sell their wares at the IETF.
sections.eli5: Sign up early, talk on the right mailing list, wear comfortable clothes and do your homework before the meeting. Then you will fit right in.

sections.title: RFCs, FYIs, STDs and Internet-Drafts
sections.content:
The memo explains that RFCs began as messages between ARPANET architects and gradually became formal, to the point of being cited as standards even when they were not. Internet Experiment Notes (IEN) were created as an informal series partly to prevent that. Two sub-series now exist within the RFCs: FYI documents, which cover overviews and introductory material, and STD documents, which identify RFCs that specify full Internet Standards. FYI and STD numbers never change across a revision, while the RFC number does.

Internet-Drafts are working documents of the IETF. An Internet-Draft is valid for six months, may be updated, replaced or obsoleted at any time, and should not be cited except as a work in progress. For more reading the memo points to RFC 1111, RFC 1150, RFC 1311, RFC 1160 and RFC 1310.
sections.eli5: RFCs are like notes passed around by the people who build the Internet. Drafts are rough copies that can change any day, so you should not treat them as final.
